# Acid-Base Disorders: Thresholds and Compensation Formulas

## Normal arterial reference ranges

Normal arterial blood gas values are pH 7.35 to 7.45, PaCO2 35 to 45 mmHg, and HCO3- 22 to 26 mEq/L. Acidaemia is defined as pH <7.35 and alkalaemia as pH >7.45. Always evaluate the primary disorder first, then check whether compensation matches the expected formula; compensation never fully normalises pH except possibly in mild chronic respiratory alkalosis.

## Anion gap and albumin correction

Calculate the serum anion gap in every metabolic acidosis:

$$
\text{AG} = \text{Na}^+ - (\text{Cl}^- + \text{HCO}_3^-)
$$

The normal anion gap is 8 to 12 mEq/L. Because albumin is the major unmeasured anion, hypoalbuminaemia hides an elevated anion gap: add 2.5 mEq/L to the observed anion gap for every 1.0 g/dL decrease in serum albumin below 4.0 g/dL:

$$
\text{AG}_{\text{corrected}} = \text{AG}_{\text{measured}} + 2.5 \times (4.0 - \text{Albumin}_{\text{g/dL}})
$$

High anion gap metabolic acidosis (AG >12 mEq/L) includes methanol, uraemia, diabetic ketoacidosis, propylene glycol, isoniazid or iron, lactic acidosis, ethylene glycol, and salicylates. Normal anion gap (hyperchloraemic) metabolic acidosis results from renal tubular acidosis, diarrhoea, or excessive 0.9% saline infusion.

## Expected compensation formulas

In metabolic acidosis, Winter's formula predicts respiratory compensation:

$$
\text{Expected } PaCO_2 = 1.5 \times [\text{HCO}_3^-] + 8 \pm 2\text{ mmHg}
$$

If measured PaCO2 is higher than Winter's upper limit, a concomitant respiratory acidosis is present; if lower than the lower limit, a concomitant respiratory alkalosis is present.

In metabolic alkalosis, PaCO2 rises by approximately 0.7 mmHg for each 1 mEq/L increase in HCO3- above 24 mEq/L (typically capped below 55 mmHg because hypoxaemia limits hypoventilation).

For primary respiratory disorders, renal HCO3- compensation depends on chronicity:

| Primary disorder | Acute change in HCO3- per 10 mmHg PaCO2 | Chronic (>3-5 days) change in HCO3- per 10 mmHg PaCO2 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Respiratory acidosis (PaCO2 ↑) | ↑ 1 mEq/L | ↑ 3.5 to 4 mEq/L |
| Respiratory alkalosis (PaCO2 ↓) | ↓ 2 mEq/L | ↓ 4 to 5 mEq/L |

## Delta-delta ratio and pitfalls

In high anion gap metabolic acidosis, calculate the delta-delta ratio to uncover hidden mixed metabolic disorders:

$$
\frac{\Delta \text{AG}}{\Delta \text{HCO}_3^-} = \frac{\text{AG}_{\text{corrected}} - 12}{24 - [\text{HCO}_3^-]}
$$

A ratio <1 indicates a concurrent non-anion-gap metabolic acidosis; a ratio between 1 and 2 indicates a pure high anion gap metabolic acidosis; a ratio >2 indicates a concurrent metabolic alkalosis or pre-existing chronic respiratory acidosis.

Do not assume a normal pH excludes an acid-base disorder: a normal pH with abnormal PaCO2 and HCO3- proves a mixed disorder. Do not rapidly overcorrect chronic respiratory acidosis with aggressive mechanical ventilation, because post-hypercapnic metabolic alkalosis can precipitate arrhythmias and seizures.
